{"markdown": "Ongoing monitoring evaluates the extent to which a model continues to perform as expected given potential changes in products, exposures, activities, clients, data relevance, or market conditions [[reg:SR26-2:V.2]].
The program recommended here tracks the same quantities this validation recomputed, against the same declared bounds, so that a monitoring report and this report can be read on one scale rather than on two.

### Quantities, frequency, and bounds

Rank-ordering power on each production vintage should be recomputed once the performance window has closed and compared against the declared floor of 0.7 [[art:8bfd02cc:threshold.package.auc.test.min]], with the held-out value of 0.748 [[art:5c6c2bfc:metrics.test.auc]] serving as the reference point established at validation.
Because that held-out value sits close to the floor, a monitoring plan should treat a sustained decline across consecutive vintages as a trigger for review well before the floor itself is reached.
Mean squared error of the predicted probabilities should be recomputed on the same schedule and compared against the declared ceiling of 0.2 [[art:d0f98b9c:threshold.package.brier.test.max]], with 0.1489 [[art:bbe69430:metrics.test.brier]] as the reference.
The slope of the outcome regressed on the log-odds of the prediction should be recomputed each vintage and held inside the declared band running from 0.8 [[art:95fdb848:threshold.package.calibration_slope.test.min]] to 1.2 [[art:0adb7a89:threshold.package.calibration_slope.test.max]], against a validation reference of 1.003 [[art:b7dbb687:calibration_slope.test]].
A slope drifting toward either edge of that band is the earliest signal that recalibration rather than redevelopment is the proportionate response, and outcomes analysis of this kind is what distinguishes an isolated deviation from a persistent one [[reg:SR26-2:V.1.b]].
Population and score stability should be measured more often than performance, on a monthly scoring cadence, since drift can be observed without waiting for outcomes to mature.
The largest per-variable stability index, score included, should be compared against the declared ceiling of 0.25 [[art:fbb5a9d1:threshold.package.psi.max]], with the train-to-test reading of 0.01095 [[art:381b2570:psi.max]] as the baseline; that baseline is small enough that any material movement in production deserves attention long before the ceiling is approached.

### Ordering of the monitoring report

An earlier section of this report presented discrimination before calibration because the observed event rate on the evaluation split is at or above 0.05 [[art:42f1351e:rule.calibration_first_event_rate]].
If a future production cohort realizes an event rate below that bound, the monitoring report for that cohort should lead with calibration and treat discrimination as the secondary lens, since rank-ordering statistics become unstable as events thin out.

### Benchmarking that this validation could not supply

This validation compared a challenger against the champion on the development data, and that comparison is reported in the benchmarking section above.
What monitoring adds is a comparison the development data cannot give: a benchmark against an external vendor or credit-bureau reference score, applied to the same production population and the same realized outcomes.
Discrepancies against such a reference warrant investigation into their source and degree rather than automatic revision, since the reference is itself an alternative prediction built on different data and methods [[reg:SR11-7:V.1.b]].

### Limitations for monitoring to carry

This validation observed the model on a static held-out split, so monitoring must carry the questions that only production can answer.
Process verification should confirm that the deployed scoring code, the upstream feature pipeline, and the data feeds behave as the packaged artifact does, and that changes to any of them are logged and reviewed.
Back-testing against realized defaults over the full performance horizon is outside what a development split can demonstrate, and should be established as a standing exercise supplemented by shorter-horizon early-warning metrics.
Overrides of the model output by users should be logged, and both their rate and their realized performance should be analyzed, since a high override rate or overrides that consistently improve outcomes points to a model in need of revision.
Segments that are thin or absent in the evaluation split should be tracked separately in production, because stability and performance measured on the population as a whole can mask deterioration confined to a subpopulation.
Macroeconomic and portfolio-mix shifts fall outside the conditions represented in the development sample, so the monitoring plan should state the range of conditions under which the model is considered applicable and flag when that range is approached or exceeded [[reg:SR26-2:V]]."}

You are drafting one section of a model-validation report on the model package credit_default version
1.0. The report follows the structure of the Federal Reserve's model risk management
guidance and never claims compliance with it.

Section: ## 7. Ongoing monitoring recommendations

What this section must do:
Recommend ongoing monitoring: which quantities to track, at what frequency, and against which
bound -- citing the same threshold artifacts the checks used rather than inventing new numbers --
and name anything this validation could not cover that monitoring should watch instead.
Section 4 of this report reported **discrimination before calibration**, because the observed event rate on the evaluation split is at or above rule.calibration_first_event_rate. You may recommend that a monitoring report lead with calibration for a future cohort whose rate falls below that bound, but do **not** write that this report led with calibration: it did not.
A challenger model was compared with the champion in this validation and section 2 reports the comparison, so do not write that benchmarking against an alternative model was not part of it. What monitoring adds is a comparison the development data cannot give: a benchmark against an external or vendor reference, or against the challenger refitted on production vintages. Say which of those you mean.

Rules, all of them checked after you answer:
- Every number you write is followed immediately by its [[art:...]] citation, copied exactly from
  the JSON below. A number with no citation is counted against this report.
- Write no number that is not in the JSON below. If you want to say something the artifacts do not
  support, say it in words without a number.
- The artifacts below are **this section's selection, not the store**. Never write that a quantity
  is absent, uncomputed, not recomputed, not available or "not carried": another section may hold
  it, and a report that says one section's selection is the whole run contradicts itself. Say what
  the numbers you have show, and where you need one you were not given, write the sentence without
  it.
- Do not write an artifact's logical name in the prose. The citation after the number carries it,
  and a sentence that also spells it out reads "by up to threshold.O1.slice_auc_gap at 0.08" where
  it should read "by up to 0.08 [[art:...:threshold.O1.slice_auc_gap]]". Say in words what the
  number is, and let the citation say where it came from.
- One sentence per line. The claim extractor works line by line, so a sentence split over two
  lines is two claims and a paragraph on one line is one.
- For a table artifact, do not retype the cells. Write the directive [[table:<logical_name>]] on a
  line of its own; the renderer expands it, with its caption and its citation, from the store.
- Open the section with a sentence that anchors it to the guidance, carrying one [[reg:...]]
  citation copied from the guidance spans below. Prefer a span of the current guidance, SR26-2;
  cite the superseded SR11-7 only where it says something the revision does not.
- Write markdown. Do not write a level-2 heading: the renderer writes it.
- Do not use the words "compliant" or "certified".
- Call something a finding only if it is in the candidate list at the end of this prompt. The
  findings section reports exactly that list, and a section that calls anything else a finding
  contradicts it.

[
 {
  "citation": "[[reg:SR26-2:V.2]]",
  "heading": "Ongoing Model Monitoring",
  "text": "Ongoing model monitoring involves an evaluation of the extent to which a model is
performing as expected given potential changes in products, exposures, activities, clients, data
relevance, or market conditions. A model that no longer performs as expected may warrant
overlays, adjustment, or redevelopment of the model depending on a banking organization’s
model risk management policy as it pertains to model deterioration.
An effective ongoing monitoring plan may also include regularly assessing any model
limitations at the development stage and over time, along with procedures for responding to any
issues that may occur, before and after a model is approved for use. The frequency and scope of
monitoring reports will depend on the nature of the model, the availability of new data or
modeling approaches, and model materiality."
 },
 {
  "citation": "[[reg:SR26-2:V]]",
  "heading": "Model Validation and Monitoring",
  "text": "Model validation evaluates whether models perform as expected and includes an
assessment of a model’s reliability and its limitations. The nature and rigor of validation generally
align with the model’s approach, use, and materiality. Sound validation identifies model
limitations and errors and clarifies appropriate use and whether corrective actions may be
warranted.
Validation provides insight into the reliability of a given model, based on its underlying
assumptions, methods, data, and relevant theories, as appropriate. This understanding helps
characterize the source and extent of the model risk. Validation can reveal performance
deterioration over time and inform judgments about acceptable performance ranges. When
performance deviates meaningfully from expectations, banking organizations generally consider
whether model adjustments, recalibration, or redevelopment are warranted.
The timing, nature, and frequency of validation activities vary based on model purpose,
model methodology, frequency and scope of model changes, data limitations, and other practical
constraints. Sound practice recognizes that validation approaches may differ across models based
on their characteristics and use. Validation generally occurs prior to a model’s first use.
However, certain circumstances (e.g., an urgent business need) may necessitate using the model
before validation is completed. In those cases, sound practice involves greater attention to the
model’s limitations when considering the appropriateness of its use, informing relevant
stakeholders of those limitations, and determining appropriate controls (e.g., placing limits on
model use or more closely monitoring its performance).
The quality of validation process depends on the rigor and effectiveness of the review
rather than on organizational structure of the banking organization’s risk management function.
Technical knowledge and modeling expertise enable appropriate analysis, meaningful critique,
and sound judgment about model performance and risk.
Even with sound modeling practices and rigorous validation, material model risk can
remain. Users of model output benefit from understanding and communicating limitations,
monitoring performance, periodically reviewing relevance, and supplementing model output
with complementary analysis and information."
 },
 {
  "citation": "[[reg:SR26-2:V.1.b]]",
  "heading": "Outcomes Analysis",
  "text": "Outcomes analysis compares model outputs to corresponding real-world outcomes to
assess model performance relative to model objectives and business use. Outcomes analysis and
other elements of the validation process may identify material errors or persistent deviations
outside of the banking organization’s established performance thresholds. In such cases, model
adjustment, recalibration, or redevelopment may be warranted.
Outcomes analysis can take many forms, including testing conducted during model
development, reports or analysis performed as part of ongoing monitoring, or standalone
activities such as back-testing or outlier analysis. A banking organization’s approach depends on
the model’s objectives, methodology, and data availability. As part of model validation, sound
practice involves reviewing outcomes analysis to evaluate the reasonableness and
appropriateness of the results, with additional analysis and testing, if warranted. When a model’s
design relies substantially on expert judgment, quantitative outcomes analysis helps to evaluate
the quality of that judgment."
 },
 {
  "citation": "[[reg:SR11-7:V.1.b]]",
  "heading": "Ongoing Monitoring",
  "text": "The second core element of the validation process is ongoing monitoring. Such
monitoring confirms that the model is appropriately implemented and is being used and is
performing as intended.
Ongoing monitoring is essential to evaluate whether changes in products, exposures,
activities, clients, or market conditions necessitate adjustment, redevelopment, or
replacement of the model and to verify that any extension of the model beyond its
original scope is valid. Any model limitations identified in the development stage should
be regularly assessed over time, as part of ongoing monitoring. Monitoring begins when a
model is first implemented in production systems for actual business use. This
monitoring should continue periodically over time, with a frequency appropriate to the
nature of the model, the availability of new data or modeling approaches, and the
magnitude of the risk involved. Banks should design a program of ongoing testing and
evaluation of model performance along with procedures for responding to any problems
that appear. This program should include process verification and benchmarking.
Process verification checks that all model components are functioning as designed. It
includes verifying that internal and external data inputs continue to be accurate, complete,
consistent with model purpose and design, and of the highest quality available. Computer
code implementing the model should be subject to rigorous quality and change control
procedures to ensure that the code is correct, that it cannot be altered except by approved
parties, and that all changes are logged and can be audited. System integration can be a
challenge and deserves special attention because the model processing component often
draws from various sources of data, processes large amounts of data, and then feeds into
multiple data repositories and reporting systems. User-developed applications, such as
spreadsheets or ad hoc database applications used to generate quantitative estimates, are
particularly prone to model risk. As the content or composition of information changes
over time, systems may need to be updated to reflect any changes in the data or its use.
Reports derived from model outputs should be reviewed as part of validation to verify
that they are accurate, complete, and informative, and that they contain appropriate
indicators of model performance and limitations.
Many of the tests employed as part of model development should be included in ongoing
monitoring and be conducted on a regular basis to incorporate additional information as it
becomes available. New empirical evidence or theoretical research may suggest the need
to modify or even replace original methods. Analysis of the integrity and applicability of [Page Break]
internal and external information sources, including information provided by third-party
vendors, should be performed regularly.
Sensitivity analysis and other checks for robustness and stability should likewise be
repeated periodically. They can be as useful during ongoing monitoring as they are
during model development. If models only work well for certain ranges of input values,
market conditions, or other factors, they should be monitored to identify situations where
these constraints are approached or exceeded.
Ongoing monitoring should include the analysis of overrides with appropriate
documentation. In the use of virtually any model, there will be cases where model output
is ignored, altered, or reversed based on the expert judgment of model users. Such
overrides are an indication that, in some respect, the model is not performing as intended
or has limitations. Banks should evaluate the reasons for overrides and track and analyze
override performance. If the rate of overrides is high, or if the override process
consistently improves model performance, it is often a sign that the underlying model
needs revision or redevelopment.
Benchmarking is the comparison of a given model's inputs and outputs to estimates from
alternative internal or external data or models. It can be incorporated in model
development as well as in ongoing monitoring. For credit risk models, examples of
benchmarks include models from vendor firms or industry consortia and data from retail
credit bureaus. Pricing models for securities and derivatives often can be compared with
alternative models that are more accurate or comprehensive but also too time consuming
to run on a daily basis. Whatever the source, benchmark models should be rigorous and
benchmark data should be accurate and complete to ensure a reasonable comparison.
Discrepancies between the model output and benchmarks should trigger investigation
into the sources and degree of the differences, and examination of whether they are
within an expected or appropriate range given the nature of the comparison. The results
of that analysis may suggest revisions to the model. However, differences do not
necessarily indicate that the model is in error. The benchmark itself is an alternative
prediction, and the differences may be due to the different data or methods used. If the
model and the benchmark match well, that is evidence in favor of the model, but it should
be interpreted with caution so the bank does not get a false degree of comfort."
 },
 {
  "citation": "[[reg:SR11-7:V.2]]",
  "heading": "Validation of Vendor and Other Third-Party Products",
  "text": "The widespread use of vendor and other third-party products—including data, parameter
values, and complete models—poses unique challenges for validation and other model
risk management activities because the modeling expertise is external to the user and
because some components are considered proprietary. Vendor products should
nevertheless be incorporated into a bank's broader model risk management framework
following the same principles as applied to in-house models, although the process may be
somewhat modified. [Page Break]
As a first step, banks should ensure that there are appropriate processes in place for
selecting vendor models. Banks should require the vendor to provide developmental
evidence explaining the product components, design, and intended use, to determine
whether the model is appropriate for the bank's products, exposures, and risks. Vendors
should provide appropriate testing results that show their product works as expected.
They should also clearly indicate the model's limitations and assumptions and where the
product's use may be problematic. Banks should expect vendors to conduct ongoing
performance monitoring and outcomes analysis, with disclosure to their clients, and to
make appropriate modifications and updates over time.
Banks are expected to validate their own use of vendor products. External models may
not allow full access to computer coding and implementation details, so the bank may
have to rely more on sensitivity analysis and benchmarking. Vendor models are often
designed to provide a range of capabilities and so may need to be customized by a bank
for its particular circumstances. A bank's customization choices should be documented
and justified as part of validation. If vendors provide input data or assumptions, or use
them to build models, their relevance for the bank's situation should be investigated.
Banks should obtain information regarding the data used to develop the model and assess
the extent to which that data is representative of the bank's situation. The bank also
should conduct ongoing monitoring and outcomes analysis of vendor model performance
using the bank's own outcomes.
Systematic procedures for validation help the bank to understand the vendor product and
its capabilities, applicability, and limitations. Such detailed knowledge is necessary for
basic controls of bank operations. It is also very important for the bank to have as much
knowledge in-house as possible, in case the vendor or the bank terminates the contract for
any reason, or if the vendor is no longer in business. Banks should have contingency
plans for instances when the vendor model is no longer available or cannot be supported
by the vendor."
 },
 {
  "citation": "[[reg:SR11-7:V.1.c]]",
  "heading": "Outcomes Analysis",
  "text": "The third core element of the validation process is outcomes analysis, a comparison of
model outputs to corresponding actual outcomes. The precise nature of the comparison
depends on the objectives of a model, and might include an assessment of the accuracy of
estimates or forecasts, an evaluation of rank-ordering ability, or other appropriate tests. In
all cases, such comparisons help to evaluate model performance, by establishing expected
ranges for those actual outcomes in relation to the intended objectives and assessing the
reasons for observed variation between the two. If outcomes analysis produces evidence
of poor performance, the bank should take action to address those issues. Outcomes
analysis typically relies on statistical tests or other quantitative measures. It can also [Page Break]
include expert judgment to check the intuition behind the outcomes and confirm that the
results make sense. When a model itself relies on expert judgment, quantitative outcomes
analysis helps to evaluate the quality of that judgment. Outcomes analysis should be
conducted on an ongoing basis to test whether the model continues to perform in line
with design objectives and business uses.
A variety of quantitative and qualitative testing and analytical techniques can be used in
outcomes analysis. The choice of technique should be based on the model's
methodology, its complexity, data availability, and the magnitude of potential model risk
to the bank. Outcomes analysis should involve a range of tests because any individual test
will have weaknesses. For example, some tests are better at checking a model's ability to
rank-order or segment observations on a relative basis, whereas others are better at
checking absolute forecast accuracy. Tests should be designed for each situation, as not
all will be effective or feasible in every circumstance, and attention should be paid to
choosing the appropriate type of outcomes analysis for a particular model.
Models are regularly adjusted to take into account new data or techniques, or because of
deterioration in performance. Parallel outcomes analysis, under which both the original
and adjusted models' forecasts are tested against realized outcomes, provides an
important test of such model adjustments. If the adjusted model does not outperform the
original model, developers, users, and reviewers should realize that additional changes—
or even a wholesale redesign—are likely necessary before the adjusted model replaces
the original one.
Back-testing is one form of outcomes analysis; specifically, it involves the comparison of
actual outcomes with model forecasts during a sample time period not used in model
development and at an observation frequency that matches the forecast horizon or
performance window of the model. The comparison is generally done using expected
ranges or statistical confidence intervals around the model forecasts. When outcomes fall
outside those intervals, the bank should analyze the discrepancies and investigate the
causes that are significant in terms of magnitude or frequency. The objective of the
analysis is to determine whether differences stem from the omission of material factors
from the model, whether they arise from errors with regard to other aspects of model
specification such as interaction terms or assumptions of linearity, or whether they are
purely random and thus consistent with acceptable model performance. Analysis of in-
sample fit and of model performance in holdout samples (data set aside and not used to
estimate the original model) are important parts of model development but are not
substitutes for back-testing.
A well-known example of back-testing is the evaluation of value-at-risk (VaR), in which
actual profit and loss is compared with a model forecast loss distribution. Significant
deviation in expected versus actual performance and unexplained volatility in the profits
and losses of trading activities may indicate that hedging and pricing relationships are not
adequately measured by a given approach. Along with measuring the frequency of losses
in excess of a single VaR percentile estimator, banks should use other tests, such as [Page Break]
assessing any clustering of exceptions and checking the distribution of losses against
other estimated percentiles.
Analysis of the results of even high-quality and well-designed back-testing can pose
challenges, since it is not a straightforward, mechanical process that always produces
unambiguous results. The purpose is to test the model, not individual forecast values.
Back-testing may entail analysis of a large number of forecasts over different conditions
at a point in time or over multiple time periods. Statistical testing is essential in such
cases, yet such testing can pose challenges in both the choice of appropriate tests and the
interpretation of results; banks should support and document both the choice of tests and
the interpretation of results.
Models with long forecast horizons should be back-tested, but given the amount of time it
would take to accumulate the necessary data, that testing should be supplemented by
evaluation over shorter periods. Banks should employ outcomes analysis consisting of
"early warning" metrics designed to measure performance beginning very shortly after
model introduction and trend analysis of performance over time. These outcomes analysis
tools are not substitutes for back-testing, which should still be performed over the longer
time period, but rather very important complements.
Outcomes analysis and the other elements of the validation process may reveal significant
errors or inaccuracies in model development or outcomes that consistently fall outside the
bank's predetermined thresholds of acceptability. In such cases, model adjustment,
recalibration, or redevelopment is warranted. Adjustments and recalibration should be
governed by the principle of conservatism and should undergo independent review.
Material changes in model structure or technique, and all model redevelopment, should
be subject to validation activities of appropriate range and rigor before implementation.

testing or sensitivity analysis for various reasons, such as lack of data or of price
observability. In those cases, even more attention should be paid to the model's
limitations when considering the appropriateness of model usage, and senior management
should be fully informed of those limitations when using the models for decision making.

{"markdown": "Ongoing monitoring evaluates the extent to which a model continues to perform as expected given potential changes in products, exposures, activities, clients, data relevance, or market conditions, and the recommendations below are framed on that basis [[reg:SR26-2:V.2]].
The quantities recommended for tracking are the ones this validation already bounded, so that each monitoring report can be read against the limits the package declares rather than against limits invented at monitoring time.

### Quantities, frequencies, and bounds

Track rank-ordering on each production cohort once its performance window has closed, against the declared floor of 0.7 [[art:8bfd02cc:threshold.package.auc.test.min]], which is the same bound the evaluation-split value of 0.748 [[art:5c6c2bfc:metrics.test.auc]] was measured against.
A quarterly cadence is appropriate for this measure, because outcomes accumulate slowly and a shorter window would report noise rather than deterioration.
Track the mean squared error of the predicted probabilities on the same quarterly cadence, against the declared ceiling of 0.2 [[art:d0f98b9c:threshold.package.brier.test.max]], the bound behind the evaluation-split value of 0.1489 [[art:bbe69430:metrics.test.brier]].
Track the slope of the logistic regression of the realized outcome on the model's log-odds for each closed cohort, against the declared band running from 0.8 [[art:95fdb848:threshold.package.calibration_slope.test.min]] to 1.2 [[art:0adb7a89:threshold.package.calibration_slope.test.max]], the band within which the evaluation-split value of 1.003 [[art:b7dbb687:calibration_slope.test]] sits.
A slope drifting toward either edge of that band is the earliest quantitative signal that the score's absolute level, rather than its ordering, has moved.
Track population stability of the scored inputs and of the score itself against the most recent approved reference sample, on a monthly cadence, against the declared ceiling of 0.25 [[art:fbb5a9d1:threshold.package.psi.max]].
Monthly is the right cadence here because drift is observable without waiting for outcomes, and the train-to-test movement of 0.01095 [[art:381b2570:psi.max]] gives a quiet baseline against which even modest production movement will be visible well before the ceiling is approached.
When any of these measures crosses its declared bound, or approaches it persistently across consecutive reports, the response should be an investigation of the source followed by a decision on overlay, recalibration, or redevelopment [[reg:SR26-2:V.1.b]].

### Ordering of the monitoring report

The presentation rule keyed to the observed event rate should carry into monitoring: for a future cohort whose event rate falls below 0.05 [[art:42f1351e:rule.calibration_first_event_rate]], the monitoring report for that cohort should lead with calibration and place discrimination after it.
Section 4 of this report presented discrimination first, because the evaluation split's event rate is at or above that bound, so a change of ordering in a later monitoring report is a signal about the cohort rather than an inconsistency with this validation.

### Benchmarking that monitoring adds

Section 2 compares a challenger against the champion on the development data, and monitoring should extend that comparison in a direction the development data cannot reach: the challenger refitted on successive production vintages and scored against the champion on the same live cohort.
Refitting on production vintages separates deterioration caused by a changed population from deterioration caused by a model specification that no longer fits, which a challenger frozen at development time cannot distinguish.
Where the refitted challenger materially outperforms the champion on realized outcomes across more than one vintage, that is grounds for redevelopment rather than for an overlay, and the comparison should be documented with the same rigor as the original development testing [[reg:SR11-7:V.1.b]].

### What monitoring must watch that this validation could not

This validation observed the model on a fixed evaluation split, so performance on cohorts booked after that split is something only back-testing over closed performance windows can establish.
Monitoring should therefore treat out-of-time outcomes analysis as the primary evidence of continued fitness, with the split-based measures above serving as the reference point rather than as a substitute [[reg:SR11-7:V.1.c]].
Override behavior lies outside what a scored evaluation split can show, and monitoring should record the rate of overrides, the reasons given, and whether overridden decisions outperform the model's own output, since a high or systematically corrective override rate points to a specification that needs revision.
Implementation in production systems is likewise outside the reach of a validation run on prepared data, so process verification of the scoring pipeline, the upstream feeds, and change control over the deployed code belongs in the monitoring program.
Segments that are thinly represented in the development population may become material in production, and monitoring should report the tracked measures by segment as those populations grow rather than only in aggregate.
Macroeconomic conditions that differ from those embedded in the development sample will not announce themselves in the score distribution alone, so the monitoring plan should pair the stability measures above with a periodic reassessment of whether the model's assumptions still hold for current conditions.
Finally, the declared bounds themselves should be revisited annually alongside the model's stated use, because a limit that was appropriate at approval may be too loose or too tight once realized production performance is available [[reg:SR26-2:V]]."}

You are drafting one section of a model-validation report on the model package credit_default version
1.0. The report follows the structure of the Federal Reserve's model risk management
guidance and never claims compliance with it.

Section: ## 7. Ongoing monitoring recommendations

What this section must do:
Recommend ongoing monitoring: which quantities to track, at what frequency, and against which
bound -- citing the same threshold artifacts the checks used rather than inventing new numbers --
and name anything this validation could not cover that monitoring should watch instead.
Section 4 of this report reported **discrimination before calibration**, because the observed event rate on the evaluation split is at or above rule.calibration_first_event_rate. You may recommend that a monitoring report lead with calibration for a future cohort whose rate falls below that bound, but do **not** write that this report led with calibration: it did not.
A challenger model was compared with the champion in this validation and section 2 reports the comparison, so do not write that benchmarking against an alternative model was not part of it. What monitoring adds is a comparison the development data cannot give: a benchmark against an external or vendor reference, or against the challenger refitted on production vintages. Say which of those you mean.

Rules, all of them checked after you answer:
- Every number you write is followed immediately by its [[art:...]] citation, copied exactly from
  the JSON below. A number with no citation is counted against this report.
- Write no number that is not in the JSON below. If you want to say something the artifacts do not
  support, say it in words without a number.
- The artifacts below are **this section's selection, not the store**. Never write that a quantity
  is absent, uncomputed, not recomputed, not available or "not carried": another section may hold
  it, and a report that says one section's selection is the whole run contradicts itself. Say what
  the numbers you have show, and where you need one you were not given, write the sentence without
  it.
- Do not write an artifact's logical name in the prose. The citation after the number carries it,
  and a sentence that also spells it out reads "by up to threshold.O1.slice_auc_gap at 0.08" where
  it should read "by up to 0.08 [[art:...:threshold.O1.slice_auc_gap]]". Say in words what the
  number is, and let the citation say where it came from.
- One sentence per line. The claim extractor works line by line, so a sentence split over two
  lines is two claims and a paragraph on one line is one.
- For a table artifact, do not retype the cells. Write the directive [[table:<logical_name>]] on a
  line of its own; the renderer expands it, with its caption and its citation, from the store.
- Open the section with a sentence that anchors it to the guidance, carrying one [[reg:...]]
  citation copied from the guidance spans below. Prefer a span of the current guidance, SR26-2;
  cite the superseded SR11-7 only where it says something the revision does not.
- Write markdown. Do not write a level-2 heading: the renderer writes it.
- Do not use the words "compliant" or "certified".
- Call something a finding only if it is in the candidate list at the end of this prompt. The
  findings section reports exactly that list, and a section that calls anything else a finding
  contradicts it.

As  part  of  model  validation,  sound\npractice  involves  reviewing  outcomes  analysis  to  evaluate  the  reasonableness  and\nappropriateness  of  the  results,  with  additional  analysis  and  testing,  if  warranted.  When  a  model\u2019s\ndesign  relies  substantially  on  expert  judgment,  quantitative  outcomes  analysis  helps  to  evaluate\nthe  quality  of  that  judgment."
 },
 {
  "citation": "[[reg:SR11-7:V.1.b]]",
  "heading": "Ongoing Monitoring",
  "text": "The  second  core  element  of  the  validation  process  is  ongoing  monitoring.  Such\nmonitoring  confirms  that  the  model  is  appropriately  implemented  and  is  being  used  and  is\nperforming  as  intended.\nOngoing  monitoring  is  essential  to  evaluate  whether  changes  in  products,  exposures,\nactivities,  clients,  or  market  conditions  necessitate  adjustment,  redevelopment,  or\nreplacement  of  the  model  and  to  verify  that  any  extension  of  the  model  beyond  its\noriginal  scope  is  valid.  Any  model  limitations  identified  in  the  development  stage  should\nbe  regularly  assessed  over  time,  as  part  of  ongoing  monitoring.  Monitoring  begins  when  a\nmodel  is  first  implemented  in  production  systems  for  actual  business  use.  This\nmonitoring  should  continue  periodically  over  time,  with  a  frequency  appropriate  to  the\nnature  of  the  model,  the  availability  of  new  data  or  modeling  approaches,  and  the\nmagnitude  of  the  risk  involved.  Banks  should  design  a  program  of  ongoing  testing  and\nevaluation  of  model  performance  along  with  procedures  for  responding  to  any  problems\nthat  appear.  This  program  should  include  process  verification  and  benchmarking.\nProcess  verification  checks  that  all  model  components  are  functioning  as  designed.  It\nincludes  verifying  that  internal  and  external  data  inputs  continue  to  be  accurate,  complete,\nconsistent  with  model  purpose  and  design,  and  of  the  highest  quality  available.  Computer\ncode  implementing  the  model  should  be  subject  to  rigorous  quality  and  change  control\nprocedures  to  ensure  that  the  code  is  correct,  that  it  cannot  be  altered  except  by  approved\nparties,  and  that  all  changes  are  logged  and  can  be  audited.  System  integration  can  be  a\nchallenge  and  deserves  special  attention  because  the  model  processing  component  often\ndraws  from  various  sources  of  data,  processes  large  amounts  of  data,  and  then  feeds  into\nmultiple  data  repositories  and  reporting  systems.  User-developed  applications,  such  as\nspreadsheets  or  ad  hoc  database  applications  used  to  generate  quantitative  estimates,  are\nparticularly  prone  to  model  risk.  As  the  content  or  composition  of  information  changes\nover  time,  systems  may  need  to  be  updated  to  reflect  any  changes  in  the  data  or  its  use.\nReports  derived  from  model  outputs  should  be  reviewed  as  part  of  validation  to  verify\nthat  they  are  accurate,  complete,  and  informative,  and  that  they  contain  appropriate\nindicators  of  model  performance  and  limitations.\nMany  of  the  tests  employed  as  part  of  model  development  should  be  included  in  ongoing\nmonitoring  and  be  conducted  on  a  regular  basis  to  incorporate  additional  information  as  it\nbecomes  available.  New  empirical  evidence  or  theoretical  research  may  suggest  the  need\nto  modify  or  even  replace  original  methods.  Analysis  of  the  integrity  and  applicability  of  [Page  Break]\ninternal  and  external  information  sources,  including  information  provided  by  third-party\nvendors,  should  be  performed  regularly.\nSensitivity  analysis  and  other  checks  for  robustness  and  stability  should  likewise  be\nrepeated  periodically.  They  can  be  as  useful  during  ongoing  monitoring  as  they  are\nduring  model  development.  If  models  only  work  well  for  certain  ranges  of  input  values,\nmarket  conditions,  or  other  factors,  they  should  be  monitored  to  identify  situations  where\nthese  constraints  are  approached  or  exceeded.\nOngoing  monitoring  should  include  the  analysis  of  overrides  with  appropriate\ndocumentation.  In  the  use  of  virtually  any  model,  there  will  be  cases  where  model  output\nis  ignored,  altered,  or  reversed  based  on  the  expert  judgment  of  model  users.  Such\noverrides  are  an  indication  that,  in  some  respect,  the  model  is  not  performing  as  intended\nor  has  limitations.  Banks  should  evaluate  the  reasons  for  overrides  and  track  and  analyze\noverride  performance.  If  the  rate  of  overrides  is  high,  or  if  the  override  process\nconsistently  improves  model  performance,  it  is  often  a  sign  that  the  underlying  model\nneeds  revision  or  redevelopment.\nBenchmarking  is  the  comparison  of  a  given  model's  inputs  and  outputs  to  estimates  from\nalternative  internal  or  external  data  or  models.  It  can  be  incorporated  in  model\ndevelopment  as  well  as  in  ongoing  monitoring.  For  credit  risk  models,  examples  of\nbenchmarks  include  models  from  vendor  firms  or  industry  consortia  and  data  from  retail\ncredit  bureaus.  Pricing  models  for  securities  and  derivatives  often  can  be  compared  with\nalternative  models  that  are  more  accurate  or  comprehensive  but  also  too  time  consuming\nto  run  on  a  daily  basis.  Whatever  the  source,  benchmark  models  should  be  rigorous  and\nbenchmark  data  should  be  accurate  and  complete  to  ensure  a  reasonable  comparison.\nDiscrepancies  between  the  model  output  and  benchmarks  should  trigger  investigation\ninto  the  sources  and  degree  of  the  differences,  and  examination  of  whether  they  are\nwithin  an  expected  or  appropriate  range  given  the  nature  of  the  comparison.  The  results\nof  that  analysis  may  suggest  revisions  to  the  model.  However,  differences  do  not\nnecessarily  indicate  that  the  model  is  in  error.  The  benchmark  itself  is  an  alternative\nprediction,  and  the  differences  may  be  due  to  the  different  data  or  methods  used.  If  the\nmodel  and  the  benchmark  match  well,  that  is  evidence  in  favor  of  the  model,  but  it  should\nbe  interpreted  with  caution  so  the  bank  does  not  get  a  false  degree  of  comfort."
 },
 {
  "citation": "[[reg:SR11-7:V.2]]",
  "heading": "Validation of Vendor and Other Third-Party Products",
  "text": "The  widespread  use  of  vendor  and  other  third-party  products\u2014including  data,  parameter\nvalues,  and  complete  models\u2014poses  unique  challenges  for  validation  and  other  model\nrisk  management  activities  because  the  modeling  expertise  is  external  to  the  user  and\nbecause  some  components  are  considered  proprietary.  Vendor  products  should\nnevertheless  be  incorporated  into  a  bank's  broader  model  risk  management  framework\nfollowing  the  same  principles  as  applied  to  in-house  models,  although  the  process  may  be\nsomewhat  modified.  [Page  Break]\nAs  a  first  step,  banks  should  ensure  that  there  are  appropriate  processes  in  place  for\nselecting  vendor  models.  Banks  should  require  the  vendor  to  provide  developmental\nevidence  explaining  the  product  components,  design,  and  intended  use,  to  determine\nwhether  the  model  is  appropriate  for  the  bank's  products,  exposures,  and  risks.  Vendors\nshould  provide  appropriate  testing  results  that  show  their  product  works  as  expected.\nThey  should  also  clearly  indicate  the  model's  limitations  and  assumptions  and  where  the\nproduct's  use  may  be  problematic.  Banks  should  expect  vendors  to  conduct  ongoing\nperformance  monitoring  and  outcomes  analysis,  with  disclosure  to  their  clients,  and  to\nmake  appropriate  modifications  and  updates  over  time.\nBanks  are  expected  to  validate  their  own  use  of  vendor  products.  External  models  may\nnot  allow  full  access  to  computer  coding  and  implementation  details,  so  the  bank  may\nhave  to  rely  more  on  sensitivity  analysis  and  benchmarking.  Vendor  models  are  often\ndesigned  to  provide  a  range  of  capabilities  and  so  may  need  to  be  customized  by  a  bank\nfor  its  particular  circumstances.  A  bank's  customization  choices  should  be  documented\nand  justified  as  part  of  validation.  If  vendors  provide  input  data  or  assumptions,  or  use\nthem  to  build  models,  their  relevance  for  the  bank's  situation  should  be  investigated.\nBanks  should  obtain  information  regarding  the  data  used  to  develop  the  model  and  assess\nthe  extent  to  which  that  data  is  representative  of  the  bank's  situation.  The  bank  also\nshould  conduct  ongoing  monitoring  and  outcomes  analysis  of  vendor  model  performance\nusing  the  bank's  own  outcomes.\nSystematic  procedures  for  validation  help  the  bank  to  understand  the  vendor  product  and\nits  capabilities,  applicability,  and  limitations.  Such  detailed  knowledge  is  necessary  for\nbasic  controls  of  bank  operations.  It  is  also  very  important  for  the  bank  to  have  as  much\nknowledge  in-house  as  possible,  in  case  the  vendor  or  the  bank  terminates  the  contract  for\nany  reason,  or  if  the  vendor  is  no  longer  in  business.  Banks  should  have  contingency\nplans  for  instances  when  the  vendor  model  is  no  longer  available  or  cannot  be  supported\nby  the  vendor."
 },
 {
  "citation": "[[reg:SR11-7:V.1.c]]",
  "heading": "Outcomes Analysis",
  "text": "The  third  core  element  of  the  validation  process  is  outcomes  analysis,  a  comparison  of\nmodel  outputs  to  corresponding  actual  outcomes.  The  precise  nature  of  the  comparison\ndepends  on  the  objectives  of  a  model,  and  might  include  an  assessment  of  the  accuracy  of\nestimates  or  forecasts,  an  evaluation  of  rank-ordering  ability,  or  other  appropriate  tests.  In\nall  cases,  such  comparisons  help  to  evaluate  model  performance,  by  establishing  expected\nranges  for  those  actual  outcomes  in  relation  to  the  intended  objectives  and  assessing  the\nreasons  for  observed  variation  between  the  two.  If  outcomes  analysis  produces  evidence\nof  poor  performance,  the  bank  should  take  action  to  address  those  issues.  Outcomes\nanalysis  typically  relies  on  statistical  tests  or  other  quantitative  measures.  It  can  also  [Page  Break]\ninclude  expert  judgment  to  check  the  intuition  behind  the  outcomes  and  confirm  that  the\nresults  make  sense.  When  a  model  itself  relies  on  expert  judgment,  quantitative  outcomes\nanalysis  helps  to  evaluate  the  quality  of  that  judgment.  Outcomes  analysis  should  be\nconducted  on  an  ongoing  basis  to  test  whether  the  model  continues  to  perform  in  line\nwith  design  objectives  and  business  uses.\nA  variety  of  quantitative  and  qualitative  testing  and  analytical  techniques  can  be  used  in\noutcomes  analysis.  The  choice  of  technique  should  be  based  on  the  model's\nmethodology,  its  complexity,  data  availability,  and  the  magnitude  of  potential  model  risk\nto  the  bank.  Outcomes  analysis  should  involve  a  range  of  tests  because  any  individual  test\nwill  have  weaknesses.  For  example,  some  tests  are  better  at  checking  a  model's  ability  to\nrank-order  or  segment  observations  on  a  relative  basis,  whereas  others  are  better  at\nchecking  absolute  forecast  accuracy.  Tests  should  be  designed  for  each  situation,  as  not\nall  will  be  effective  or  feasible  in  every  circumstance,  and  attention  should  be  paid  to\nchoosing  the  appropriate  type  of  outcomes  analysis  for  a  particular  model.\nModels  are  regularly  adjusted  to  take  into  account  new  data  or  techniques,  or  because  of\ndeterioration  in  performance.  Parallel  outcomes  analysis,  under  which  both  the  original\nand  adjusted  models'  forecasts  are  tested  against  realized  outcomes,  provides  an\nimportant  test  of  such  model  adjustments.  If  the  adjusted  model  does  not  outperform  the\noriginal  model,  developers,  users,  and  reviewers  should  realize  that  additional  changes\u2014\nor  even  a  wholesale  redesign\u2014are  likely  necessary  before  the  adjusted  model  replaces\nthe  original  one.\nBack-testing  is  one  form  of  outcomes  analysis;  specifically,  it  involves  the  comparison  of\nactual  outcomes  with  model  forecasts  during  a  sample  time  period  not  used  in  model\ndevelopment  and  at  an  observation  frequency  that  matches  the  forecast  horizon  or\nperformance  window  of  the  model.  The  comparison  is  generally  done  using  expected\nranges  or  statistical  confidence  intervals  around  the  model  forecasts.  When  outcomes  fall\noutside  those  intervals,  the  bank  should  analyze  the  discrepancies  and  investigate  the\ncauses  that  are  significant  in  terms  of  magnitude  or  frequency.  The  objective  of  the\nanalysis  is  to  determine  whether  differences  stem  from  the  omission  of  material  factors\nfrom  the  model,  whether  they  arise  from  errors  with  regard  to  other  aspects  of  model\nspecification  such  as  interaction  terms  or  assumptions  of  linearity,  or  whether  they  are\npurely  random  and  thus  consistent  with  acceptable  model  performance.  Analysis  of  in-\nsample  fit  and  of  model  performance  in  holdout  samples  (data  set  aside  and  not  used  to\nestimate  the  original  model)  are  important  parts  of  model  development  but  are  not\nsubstitutes  for  back-testing.\nA  well-known  example  of  back-testing  is  the  evaluation  of  value-at-risk  (VaR),  in  which\nactual  profit  and  loss  is  compared  with  a  model  forecast  loss  distribution.  Significant\ndeviation  in  expected  versus  actual  performance  and  unexplained  volatility  in  the  profits\nand  losses  of  trading  activities  may  indicate  that  hedging  and  pricing  relationships  are  not\nadequately  measured  by  a  given  approach.  Along  with  measuring  the  frequency  of  losses\nin  excess  of  a  single  VaR  percentile  estimator,  banks  should  use  other  tests,  such  as  [Page  Break]\nassessing  any  clustering  of  exceptions  and  checking  the  distribution  of  losses  against\nother  estimated  percentiles.\nAnalysis  of  the  results  of  even  high-quality  and  well-designed  back-testing  can  pose\nchallenges,  since  it  is  not  a  straightforward,  mechanical  process  that  always  produces\nunambiguous  results.  The  purpose  is  to  test  the  model,  not  individual  forecast  values.\nBack-testing  may  entail  analysis  of  a  large  number  of  forecasts  over  different  conditions\nat  a  point  in  time  or  over  multiple  time  periods.  Statistical  testing  is  essential  in  such\ncases,  yet  such  testing  can  pose  challenges  in  both  the  choice  of  appropriate  tests  and  the\ninterpretation  of  results;  banks  should  support  and  document  both  the  choice  of  tests  and\nthe  interpretation  of  results.\nModels  with  long  forecast  horizons  should  be  back-tested,  but  given  the  amount  of  time  it\nwould  take  to  accumulate  the  necessary  data,  that  testing  should  be  supplemented  by\nevaluation  over  shorter  periods.  Banks  should  employ  outcomes  analysis  consisting  of\n\"early  warning\"  metrics  designed  to  measure  performance  beginning  very  shortly  after\nmodel  introduction  and  trend  analysis  of  performance  over  time.  These  outcomes  analysis\ntools  are  not  substitutes  for  back-testing,  which  should  still  be  performed  over  the  longer\ntime  period,  but  rather  very  important  complements.\nOutcomes  analysis  and  the  other  elements  of  the  validation  process  may  reveal  significant\nerrors  or  inaccuracies  in  model  development  or  outcomes  that  consistently  fall  outside  the\nbank's  predetermined  thresholds  of  acceptability.  In  such  cases,  model  adjustment,\nrecalibration,  or  redevelopment  is  warranted.  Adjustments  and  recalibration  should  be\ngoverned  by  the  principle  of  conservatism  and  should  undergo  independent  review.\nMaterial  changes  in  model  structure  or  technique,  and  all  model  redevelopment,  should\nbe  subject  to  validation  activities  of  appropriate  range  and  rigor  before  implementation.\nAt  times  banks  may  have  a  limited  ability  to  use  key  model  validation  tools  like  back-\ntesting  or  sensitivity  analysis  for  various  reasons,  such  as  lack  of  data  or  of  price\nobservability.  In  those  cases,  even  more  attention  should  be  paid  to  the  model's\nlimitations  when  considering  the  appropriateness  of  model  usage,  and  senior  management\nshould  be  fully  informed  of  those  limitations  when  using  the  models  for  decision  making.\nSuch  scrutiny  should  be  applied  to  individual  models  and  models  in  the  aggregate.\n\n"
 }
]

{"markdown":"Ongoing monitoring evaluates the extent to which the model continues to perform as expected given potential changes in products, exposures, activities, clients, data relevance, or market conditions, and the frequency and scope of the monitoring reports recommended below are set to the model's use and materiality [[reg:SR26-2:V.2]].

### 7.1 Quantities, frequencies, and bounds

Rank-ordering power on scored production cohorts should be tracked once outcomes have matured for a cohort, and compared against the declared floor of 0.7 [[art:8bfd02cc:threshold.package.auc.test.min]], with the validation-time value of 0.748 [[art:5c6c2bfc:metrics.test.auc]] serving as the reference level from which deterioration is measured.
Probability accuracy should be tracked on the same cohort cadence against the declared ceiling of 0.2 [[art:d0f98b9c:threshold.package.brier.test.max]], with the validation-time value of 0.1489 [[art:bbe69430:metrics.test.brier]] as the reference level.
The regression slope of realized outcomes on the logit of the predicted probability should be tracked on the same cadence and held inside the declared band running from 0.8 [[art:95fdb848:threshold.package.calibration_slope.test.min]] to 1.2 [[art:0adb7a89:threshold.package.calibration_slope.test.max]], against a validation-time value of 1.003 [[art:b7dbb687:calibration_slope.test]] that sits close to the centre of that band.
Input and score distribution shift should be tracked more often than outcomes allow, on a monthly production cycle, against the declared stability ceiling of 0.25 [[art:fbb5a9d1:threshold.package.psi.max]]; the largest shift seen between the development and evaluation windows was 0.01095 [[art:381b2570:psi.max]], so the monitoring band starts with substantial headroom and any sustained move toward the ceiling is worth investigating well before it is reached.
Because shift can be measured as soon as scores are produced while the performance measures wait on outcome maturity, the monitoring plan should treat the monthly shift report as the early-warning layer and the outcome-based report as the confirming layer.

Monitoring reports should record not only whether each quantity sits inside its bound but also the direction and persistence of movement within it, since a series drifting steadily across its band carries information that a single in-bound reading does not.
Where a quantity deviates from expectation persistently rather than in a single period, the monitoring plan should route the result into a decision about overlays, adjustment, recalibration, or redevelopment rather than into a repeated exception [[reg:SR26-2:V.1.b]].

### 7.2 Report ordering

Section 4 of this report presented discrimination ahead of calibration, because the observed event rate on the evaluation split was at or above the rate of 0.05 [[art:42f1351e:rule.calibration_first_event_rate]] below which the ordering reverses.
A future monitoring report covering a production cohort whose observed event rate falls below 0.05 [[art:42f1351e:rule.calibration_first_event_rate]] may lead with calibration instead, and should say plainly which ordering it used and why, so that readers can compare cohorts without inferring the reason from the layout.

### 7.3 What monitoring adds that this validation could not

Section 2 of this report compares the champion against a challenger fitted on the same development data, and monitoring should extend that comparison in the one direction the development data cannot reach: the challenger refitted on successive production vintages, so that the comparison is re-run on data drawn from the period in which the champion is actually deciding.
A champion that keeps its edge on development data while losing it to a challenger refitted on recent vintages is showing a form of deterioration that no re-reading of the development split will surface, and discrepancies of that kind should trigger investigation into their source and degree rather than an immediate change of model.
This validation observed the model on fixed historical splits, so it speaks to behaviour on those splits and not to behaviour under the production data feeds, the production scoring path, or the decision environment in which scores are consumed; monitoring should carry process verification of the input feeds and the implemented scoring code so that a change in the pipeline is not read as a change in the population.
This validation also had no realized production outcomes to compare against, so back-testing on cohorts drawn from periods outside the development sample, at an observation frequency matched to the performance window, belongs to monitoring rather than to this report [[reg:SR11-7:V.1.c]].
Monitoring should track the rate of overrides and the performance of overridden cases with documentation of the reasons, since a high override rate or an override process that consistently improves on the model is a signal about the model itself that this validation was not positioned to observe [[reg:SR11-7:V.1.b]].
Finally, the limitations recorded elsewhere in this report should be re-assessed on the same cycle as the quantitative measures, together with the continued relevance of the model's intended population, so that scope creep in use is caught by the monitoring process rather than by an eventual performance breach [[reg:SR26-2:V]]."}

This validation observed the model on fixed historical splits, so it speaks to behaviour on those splits and not to behaviour under the production data feeds, the production scoring path, or the decision environment in which scores are consumed; monitoring should carry process verification of the input feeds and the implemented scoring code so that a change in the pipeline is not read as a change in the population.
This validation also had no realized production outcomes to compare against, so back-testing on cohorts drawn from periods outside the development sample, at an observation frequency matched to the performance window, belongs to monitoring rather than to this report [[reg:SR11-7:V.1.c]].
Monitoring should track the rate of overrides and the performance of overridden cases with documentation of the reasons, since a high override rate or an override process that consistently improves on the model is a signal about the model itself that this validation was not positioned to observe [[reg:SR11-7:V.1.b]].
Finally, the limitations recorded elsewhere in this report should be re-assessed on the same cycle as the quantitative measures, together with the continued relevance of the model's intended population, so that scope creep in use is caught by the monitoring process rather than by an eventual performance breach [[reg:SR26-2:V]]."}

results make sense. When a model itself relies on expert judgment, quantitative outcomes
analysis helps to evaluate the quality of that judgment. Outcomes analysis should be
conducted on an ongoing basis to test whether the model continues to perform in line

outcomes analysis. The choice of technique should be based on the model's
methodology, its complexity, data availability, and the magnitude of potential model risk
to the bank. Outcomes analysis should involve a range of tests because any individual test
will have weaknesses. For example, some tests are better at checking a model's ability to
rank-order or segment observations on a relative basis, whereas others are better at
checking absolute forecast accuracy. Tests should be designed for each situation, as not
all will be effective or feasible in every circumstance, and attention should be paid to
choosing the appropriate type of outcomes analysis for a particular model.

important test of such model adjustments. If the adjusted model does not outperform the
original model, developers, users, and reviewers should realize that additional changes—
or even a wholesale redesign—are likely necessary before the adjusted model replaces
the original one.

actual outcomes with model forecasts during a sample time period not used in model
development and at an observation frequency that matches the forecast horizon or
performance window of the model. The comparison is generally done using expected
ranges or statistical confidence intervals around the model forecasts. When outcomes fall
outside those intervals, the bank should analyze the discrepancies and investigate the
causes that are significant in terms of magnitude or frequency. The objective of the
analysis is to determine whether differences stem from the omission of material factors
from the model, whether they arise from errors with regard to other aspects of model

{"markdown": "Ongoing monitoring evaluates the extent to which a model continues to perform as expected given potential changes in products, exposures, activities, clients, data relevance, or market conditions, and the frequency and scope of monitoring reports depend on the nature of the model, the availability of new data or modeling approaches, and model materiality [[reg:SR26-2:V.2]].
The recommendations below reuse the bounds that the checks in this report were evaluated against, so that a monitoring report and this validation remain readable against each other.

### Quantities, frequency, and bounds

Rank-ordering on the evaluation split stood at 0.748 [[art:5c6c2bfc:metrics.test.auc]] against the declared floor of 0.7 [[art:8bfd02cc:threshold.package.auc.test.min]], and this pair should be re-reported each quarter on the newest cohort whose performance window has closed.
Probability accuracy stood at 0.1489 [[art:bbe69430:metrics.test.brier]] against the declared ceiling of 0.2 [[art:d0f98b9c:threshold.package.brier.test.max]], and the same quarterly cohort should carry it alongside the rank-ordering figure.
The regression of the outcome on the log-odds of the score gave a slope of 1.003 [[art:b7dbb687:calibration_slope.test]], which monitoring should re-estimate quarterly and read against the declared band running from 0.8 [[art:95fdb848:threshold.package.calibration_slope.test.min]] up to 1.2 [[art:0adb7a89:threshold.package.calibration_slope.test.max]].
Population stability, taken as the largest shift across the scored fields with the score itself included, stood at 0.01095 [[art:381b2570:psi.max]] against the declared ceiling of 0.25 [[art:fbb5a9d1:threshold.package.psi.max]].
Because that stability measure needs no realized outcomes, it should be computed monthly rather than quarterly, which makes it the earliest warning in the plan and the quantity most worth wiring into an automated alert.
No new bound should be introduced by the monitoring report, since the bounds above are the ones this report's checks used, and a change to any of them belongs to a package revision reviewed on its own terms rather than to a monitoring cycle.
Because a single cohort can drift outside a bound by chance or through thin volume, escalation should key on persistent deviation outside the declared bounds rather than on a lone exceedance, and a persistent deviation should prompt consideration of overlays, adjustment, recalibration, or redevelopment [[reg:SR26-2:V.1.b]].

### Ordering of the monitoring report

An earlier section of this report presented discrimination before calibration, because the observed event rate on the evaluation split sits at or above the ordering bound of 0.05 [[art:42f1351e:rule.calibration_first_event_rate]].
If a future monitored cohort has an event rate below that bound of 0.05 [[art:42f1351e:rule.calibration_first_event_rate]], the monitoring report for that cohort should lead with calibration instead, because at low event rates the calibration evidence is the more informative of the two and the rank-ordering figure becomes the noisier one.

### Benchmarking that monitoring adds

A challenger model was compared with the champion in this validation and the comparison is reported earlier, so the benchmark that monitoring adds is not a first comparison against an alternative model but one the development data cannot give: the challenger refitted on production vintages and scored against the champion on the same monitored cohort.
That refitted-challenger comparison is what is meant here, rather than an external or vendor reference, because it isolates whether the champion's fitted relationships have aged relative to a like-for-like model estimated on current data.
A gap that opens between the refitted challenger and the champion should trigger investigation into the source and degree of the difference rather than automatic replacement, since the benchmark is itself an alternative prediction and the difference may reflect the newer vintages rather than an error in the champion [[reg:SR11-7:V.1.b]].

### What monitoring should watch in place of this validation

This validation observed the model on a fixed historical split, so its evidence speaks to behavior on that split rather than to behavior on cohorts drawn after deployment, and outcomes analysis on production vintages is therefore monitoring's to carry [[reg:SR26-2:V.1.b]].
The stability measure above compares the training population with the evaluation split, so drift arising after deployment, including upstream changes to how the scored fields are populated or defaulted, has to be re-measured on each monthly cohort against the same ceiling of 0.25 [[art:fbb5a9d1:threshold.package.psi.max]].
Override behavior by model users lies outside a validation run on a static extract, so monitoring should log overrides with their stated reasons and track override outcomes, since a high override rate or an override process that consistently improves on the score indicates the underlying model needs revision [[reg:SR11-7:V.1.b]].
Process verification in the production environment is likewise monitoring's responsibility: that inputs arrive complete and on the expected scale, that the scoring code in production is the code reviewed here, and that changes to it are controlled and logged [[reg:SR11-7:V.1.b]].
Macroeconomic and portfolio-mix conditions were effectively held constant across the historical split, and a shift in either can move the relationship between the score and the outcome without moving the input distributions much, which makes the quarterly discrimination and calibration re-reports the intended detection route for that class of change.
The cadence recommended here — monthly stability, quarterly discrimination and calibration, and the refitted-challenger benchmark on the same quarterly rhythm — should be tightened if the portfolio's exposure grows or if the model is extended to a population beyond the one it was fitted on, and any such extension of scope warrants its own review before use [[reg:SR26-2:V]].
Nothing in this section is raised as a finding; these are the recommended contents of the monitoring plan.
"}

Probability accuracy stood at 0.1489 [[art:bbe69430:metrics.test.brier]] against the declared ceiling of 0.2 [[art:d0f98b9c:threshold.package.brier.test.max]], and the same quarterly cohort should carry it alongside the rank-ordering figure.
The regression of the outcome on the log-odds of the score gave a slope of 1.003 [[art:b7dbb687:calibration_slope.test]], which monitoring should re-estimate quarterly and read against the declared band running from 0.8 [[art:95fdb848:threshold.package.calibration_slope.test.min]] up to 1.2 [[art:0adb7a89:threshold.package.calibration_slope.test.max]].
Population stability, taken as the largest shift across the scored fields with the score itself included, stood at 0.01095 [[art:381b2570:psi.max]] against the declared ceiling of 0.25 [[art:fbb5a9d1:threshold.package.psi.max]].
Because that stability measure needs no realized outcomes, it should be computed monthly rather than quarterly, which makes it the earliest warning in the plan and the quantity most worth wiring into an automated alert.
No new bound should be introduced by the monitoring report, since the bounds above are the ones this report's checks used, and a change to any of them belongs to a package revision reviewed on its own terms rather than to a monitoring cycle.
Because a single cohort can drift outside a bound by chance or through thin volume, escalation should key on persistent deviation outside the declared bounds rather than on a lone exceedance, and a persistent deviation should prompt consideration of overlays, adjustment, recalibration, or redevelopment [[reg:SR26-2:V.1.b]].

### Ordering of the monitoring report

An earlier section of this report presented discrimination before calibration, because the observed event rate on the evaluation split sits at or above the ordering bound of 0.05 [[art:42f1351e:rule.calibration_first_event_rate]].
If a future monitored cohort has an event rate below that bound of 0.05 [[art:42f1351e:rule.calibration_first_event_rate]], the monitoring report for that cohort should lead with calibration instead, because at low event rates the calibration evidence is the more informative of the two and the rank-ordering figure becomes the noisier one.

### Benchmarking that monitoring adds

A challenger model was compared with the champion in this validation and the comparison is reported earlier, so the benchmark that monitoring adds is not a first comparison against an alternative model but one the development data cannot give: the challenger refitted on production vintages and scored against the champion on the same monitored cohort.
That refitted-challenger comparison is what is meant here, rather than an external or vendor reference, because it isolates whether the champion's fitted relationships have aged relative to a like-for-like model estimated on current data.
A gap that opens between the refitted challenger and the champion should trigger investigation into the source and degree of the difference rather than automatic replacement, since the benchmark is itself an alternative prediction and the difference may reflect the newer vintages rather than an error in the champion [[reg:SR11-7:V.1.b]].

### What monitoring should watch in place of this validation

This validation observed the model on a fixed historical split, so its evidence speaks to behavior on that split rather than to behavior on cohorts drawn after deployment, and outcomes analysis on production vintages is therefore monitoring's to carry [[reg:SR26-2:V.1.b]].
The stability measure above compares the training population with the evaluation split, so drift arising after deployment, including upstream changes to how the scored fields are populated or defaulted, has to be re-measured on each monthly cohort against the same ceiling of 0.25 [[art:fbb5a9d1:threshold.package.psi.max]].
Override behavior by model users lies outside a validation run on a static extract, so monitoring should log overrides with their stated reasons and track override outcomes, since a high override rate or an override process that consistently improves on the score indicates the underlying model needs revision [[reg:SR11-7:V.1.b]].
Process verification in the production environment is likewise monitoring's responsibility: that inputs arrive complete and on the expected scale, that the scoring code in production is the code reviewed here, and that changes to it are controlled and logged [[reg:SR11-7:V.1.b]].
Macroeconomic and portfolio-mix conditions were effectively held constant across the historical split, and a shift in either can move the relationship between the score and the outcome without moving the input distributions much, which makes the quarterly discrimination and calibration re-reports the intended detection route for that class of change.
The cadence recommended here — monthly stability, quarterly discrimination and calibration, and the refitted-challenger benchmark on the same quarterly rhythm — should be tightened if the portfolio's exposure grows or if the model is extended to a population beyond the one it was fitted on, and any such extension of scope warrants its own review before use [[reg:SR26-2:V]].
Nothing in this section is raised as a finding; these are the recommended contents of the monitoring plan.
"}

limitations when considering the appropriateness of model usage, and senior management
should be fully informed of those limitations when using the models for decision making.

### 7.3 What monitoring should watch that this validation could not

This validation was conducted on development and evaluation data, and several risks by their nature only become observable after the model is in production use.

- Outcomes analysis on realized production outcomes is the test this validation could only approximate with a held-out split, and back-testing over a window matching the performance horizon should begin as soon as the first cohort seasons. [[reg:SR11-7:V.1.c]]
- Process verification of the production implementation, covering the accuracy and completeness of the live input feeds and change control over the scoring code, belongs to monitoring because it concerns systems rather than the model specification reviewed here. [[reg:SR11-7:V.1.b]]
- Override behavior by model users cannot arise before deployment, and the rate of overrides together with the realized performance of overridden decisions should be tracked and documented, since a high override rate or overrides that consistently improve outcomes signals that the underlying model needs revision.
- Macroeconomic and portfolio conditions outside the range spanned by the data used here are a limitation of the development sample, and monitoring should watch for cohorts whose input ranges approach or exceed the conditions represented in that sample.

### 7.4 Benchmarking that monitoring adds

Section 2 of this report compares the champion with a challenger, and both were estimated on the same development data, so that comparison speaks to the choice of specification rather than to the model's standing against the wider market.

What monitoring adds is a benchmark against an external or vendor reference, such as a retail credit bureau score or a vendor credit scorecard, applied to the bank's own production population and scored against the bank's own realized outcomes. [[reg:SR11-7:V.1.b]]

This benchmark should be run at least annually, or sooner if a quarterly report shows a bound approached, and any discrepancy in rank-ordering or in level should trigger investigation of its source rather than an automatic conclusion that either model is in error.

Where the external reference is a vendor product, the bank should obtain the vendor's developmental evidence and its statement of limitations, and assess how far the vendor's development data represents this portfolio, before treating agreement with the benchmark as reassurance. [[reg:SR11-7:V.2]]

### 7.5 Reporting and scope

The frequency and scope proposed above reflect the nature of this model, the rate at which new outcome data becomes available, and the model's materiality, and they should be revisited if any of those change. [[reg:SR26-2:V.2]]

Model limitations identified at development and in this validation should be reassessed at each periodic review rather than treated as settled, and the monitoring report should carry the current limitation statement alongside the performance measures so that users of the output see both together. [[reg:SR26-2:V]]"}

Adjustments and recalibration should be\ngoverned by the principle of conservatism and should undergo independent review.\nMaterial changes in model structure or technique, and all model redevelopment, should\nbe subject to validation activities of appropriate range and rigor before implementation.\nAt times banks may have a limited ability to use key model validation tools like back-\ntesting or sensitivity analysis for various reasons, such as lack of data or of price\nobservability.
